## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

How did getting back to those guests go? -- All called back within the hour · All called back the same day · All called back, but only the next day or later · Some never got a callback · None got a callback; the calls were simply lost (line under the first).

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the obvious last step before the link goes to reservation agents, and it comes after the problem rows are checked.
screens.why2: The question is plain to me, and the hint covers the video, the on-screen text, the one-off 400 credits and the text-message link in words I read once.
screens.why3: I can hear both 5-second samples and judge which voice a German reservation agent on shift would take a call from, so it is my own call to make.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct and each has a sample, but nothing says whether they ask in German, which is the one thing I need to know before I send this to agents in Munich and Berlin.
screens.why5: It still says reservation agents and my questions, and nothing of Codyco's product or my roles leaks into what the respondent will hear.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ 5 s) / Saskia (German, ▶ 5 s)

screens.why1: Having just picked who asks, choosing how my reservation agents answer the link is the obvious next step before it goes out.
screens.why2: Plain words; Daphne was introduced on the screen before, and I can picture an agent between calls reading and tapping.
screens.why3: I know my agents sit at a desk or headset mid-shift, so I can judge that read-and-tap fits them better than a video interview.
screens.why4: The three choices (Daphne, read and tap, either) are complete and distinct; only 'text' in the third option names the second differently.
screens.why5: It still says reservation agents, and nothing of Codyco's AI receptionist leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: Same screen, with the third option reading 'they pick Daphne or Read and tap when they open the link' so it matches the second option's name.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how agents answer, choosing who gets the link is the obvious last step before I send the study out to the reservation agents at the groups I work with.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" is plain, and the three routes (named people, a Keel search list, one open link) read clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to: the reservation agents and desk staff at the 7 hotel groups we already work with, by name.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the real choices, but the middle option switches from "I" to "you send them" and leans on Keel's own "Contacts page", so it reads in a different voice from the other two.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco or my roles is changed or leaked; it is purely about distribution, and my pick of people I know by name is offered as written.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel contact search (I pick a list, I send each link) / A group, one open link (I post it where they already are; each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The stage verdict *Holding up* sits under the title and the tally *4 beliefs: 4 holding · 7 people answered* is tied to it by the stated rule that the verdict is the worst card, with each card's count beside its own status word.
screens.why_b2: Each card plainly says what was counted, over 7, and where the bar sits (7 of 7 · bar 6 of 7), but the Importance card prints *6 of 7 put it in their two* twice, which looks like a glitch and made me read it again.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution are my beliefs in my words (booking calls ringing out, 5 to 7 days out of 7); the Importance line just pastes my circumstance in clumsily but is still mine.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what four holding beliefs mean for Codyco or what to do next (say, move on to the solution and the €3,000 pilot); *What it measures* only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown on every line, but the page never says 7 is a small sample, and it puts my 5%-of-calls and seven-figure claim right under *Holding up* as if these answers had confirmed figures they never measured.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 reservation agents (a small sample): all 7 let a booking call ring out last week, on about 6 days in 7, and say callbacks fall short; the 5% and seven-figure figures weren't tested here, so the problem is real enough to take to the solution and the pilot.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits directly beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts who said yes, runs from 0 to 7 people with all 7 cells for me, and marks my bar at 6 of 7 (at least 8 in 10), so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The event is my own clause, a booking call rang out unanswered, but the belief line drops my segment's qualifiers (at hotel groups in Germany with a central reservations office or call center) and just says 'reservation agents'.
screens.why_b4: It says the problem is common among these 7 and sends me to the next two cards, Frequency and Importance, as the questions that decide whether this is worth selling against.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than these 7 people said.
screens.instead: Keep my full segment in the belief line ('reservation agents at hotel groups in Germany that run a central reservations office or call center') and drop the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after the yes/no question.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding numbers: 6 of 7 inside my 5 to 7 days against a bar of 5 of 7, with a median of 6 days.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7, seven people and the marker at 5 are all plain, but the legend's 'what you said' next to 'at what you said' needed a second look to tell apart, and the 0 tick sits on an axis no one could answer.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is my dimension and 5 to 7 days is my range, but 'let a booking call ring out' blames the agent where I said calls get missed after hours, at peak and on holidays, and the tail 'the most recent time it happened' doesn't fit a count of days.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' only points onward; it doesn't say that a missed booking call on nearly every day makes daily call forwarding worth pitching.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the one agent below my range is shown as counting against.
screens.instead: Asked: 'On how many of the last 7 days did a booking call ring out unanswered?'; So: 6 of 7 missed a booking call on 5 or more days, so a missed call is a near-daily event; a small group, so read it as a lean. Next: whether it matters to them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* sits right beside its deciding number: 6 of 7 put it in their two, against a bar of 5 of 7 (the count is printed twice in a row, which is only a stutter).
screens.why_b2: The caption says it plainly: 7 people, each picked two, bars count the 14 picks. My row stands at 6 against 2 for each other row, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the marker at 5.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the own row is my missed-call problem, *Picking up calls before they ring out*, set first among my five; the belief drops *at hotel groups* from my actors, but it is plainly the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line only warns that this means top two, not first; it doesn't tell me the concrete point, that missed calls beat every desk and email task for the agents. Nor does it say the one against (Chiara) is at a group whose call center already covers after hours, which is my 5%-even-with-call-centers pitch's weak spot.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line calls it a small group (*a lean, not a call*), and the So line limits the claim to *among these 7*.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 agents put missed booking calls in their top two over desk, rate and email work, a lean among 7; the one against has a call center covering after six, so test groups that already run one before you pitch them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each rung carries its count and a for/against tag, the 7 people show in the strip and the count line, and both my line under 'All called back that day' and the bar marker at 5 are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief names my act, getting back to a guest whose booking call went unanswered, and the five rungs are the ones I typed, with my line under 'All called back that day'.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic hand-off; it doesn't tell me the gap is mostly slow callbacks ('when there was time', 5 of 7), which is exactly where instant AI answering should be pitched and measured.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, everyone is listed, and the card itself says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so a clean 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: Today's way fell short for all 7 of these 7, mostly slow callbacks (5 called back only when there was time) rather than calls lost outright; a lean from 7, so on the next study test whether answering every missed call live beats a same-day callback.

screens.why_b1: The status word Holding up sits beside the deciding number, and the line 'Importance held, 6 of 7; the 1 who said no' ties it to the bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The card is Importance, and the belief is the one I checked: picking up calls before they ring out is one of the agent's two hardest things on a shift.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the one dissent means for Codyco, such as whether groups whose call center already covers after hours are a weaker first segment or whether to keep pitching central offices.
screens.why_b5: The 6 of 7, the 1 against and the single quote are all counted plainly, and nothing is claimed beyond the seven who answered.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's answer adds something I did not type: where a call center takes the phones after six, the pain moves to group emails with no rates attached, which cuts into my 'even with call centers' pitch.
screens.instead: Importance held 6 of 7 (bar 5 of 7, a small sample); the one no came from a group whose call center already covers after hours and whose pain is group emails with no rates, so test whether groups with after-hours coverage are a weaker segment before pitching them.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check straight away that I sit in a hotel group's central reservations office, since the whole study is about the calls we take there.
screens.why2: Central reservations office, call center and hotel group are exactly the words we use in the trade, and I can answer at once.
screens.why3: I work in our group's central reservations office in Munich, so I know my answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment (hotel groups in Germany with a central reservations office or call center), and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question that is easy to answer on one hearing, though 'I'll read 2 options' before a plain yes or no is a little stiff where the screener's own form is just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Same question, but spoken as: Do you work in the central reservations office or call center of a hotel group in Germany? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether a booking call went unanswered this week is the obvious first question.
screens.why2: Ring out unanswered is our everyday talk, but let makes it sound like I chose to ignore it, when at peak on a trade-fair Saturday the call just waits in the queue while I am on another line.
screens.why3: In a central office the phone system queues calls, so I often don't see which ones were abandoned (my team lead sees that on the dashboard), and I would partly be guessing whether one was mine.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is calls that do not get answered, but you let them ring out pins it on me personally, which drifts a little from the founder's words and may make some of us say No out of pride.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and Yes or no is easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: The gate asks the costly event, an unanswered booking call, not the routine of taking calls, so a colleague on a quiet week can truly say No and one on a peak shift Yes, with no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call meant for you go unanswered? Yes / No

screens.why1: I just said yes, a call rang out in the last 7 days, so asking on how many days follows straight on.
screens.why2: Booking call and ring out unanswered are how we talk in the office, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know some days rang out, but our queue holds calls and I don't see each one drop, and I don't work all 7 days, so I'd partly guess; *let* also makes it sound like my choice when it's just everyone on the line.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 plus I can't recall covers every true answer, with no overlap and no 0 after my yes.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me; it's just about calls ringing out on my shifts.
screens.why6: Short and one question, and *say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall* is easy to hold.
screens.why7: The measure is days of the window, said once in the window phrase, with buttons 1 to 7 and the one escape apart; the event is a single act that happened on a day or did not, so a founder's low of 2 or more splits the buttons for and against.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 7 days did a booking call ring out before you could pick up? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often calls rang out, it makes sense to ask how that ranks against the other hard parts of my shift.
screens.why2: Every option is how we talk in the reservations office (rate, group request, changes to a booking, a call ringing out), though *shift of booking calls* is a little stiff, since we just say *Schicht*.
screens.why3: These are all things I do myself on a busy trade-fair Saturday, so I can pick from my own last shift.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and the escape fits, but *group requests that come by email* is email work set against a shift framed as booking calls, so it sits a little apart from the rest.
screens.why5: Picking up calls before they ring out keeps the founder's hurt in my words, and nothing about a product or plan leaks to me.
screens.why6: Short stem, five parallel phrases I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The own row is there, not first and not missing, with four rivals, *None of these* at the first ask, and a belief that can go either way; but the email row drifts to another channel, which the card names as a pitfall.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the phones. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Answering guests' questions about their stay · Taking a group request over the phone · Quoting the right rate while the guest waits · Handling changes to existing bookings · Picking up calls before they ring out · None of these

screens.why1: Right after asking how often calls rang out, it makes sense to ask what we did about the ones we missed.
screens.why2: 'How did getting back to a guest whose booking call went unanswered go?' is a tangle I had to read twice, and 'your last booking call' points me at a call I actually answered, not one I missed.
screens.why3: I know roughly whether we rang back the missed numbers last Saturday, but on a trade-fair day the callback list sits with the ACD report and the team lead, so for 'all' versus 'some' I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: The stem asks about one guest but the options count many calls (every, all, some, few), and 'within the hour' versus 'that day' mixes speed with how many; still, the true answers are there and 'Someone else did it' fits, since a callback colleague often handles it.
screens.why5: Booking calls ringing out and calling guests back is how we talk in the office, and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: The five options say well as a list, but the stem is a mouthful heard once, and I'd lose the thread before the options start.
screens.why7: Five rungs run best to worst, the first one working (all called back within the hour), the last failing outright (calls simply lost), with one escape apart, so the belief can go either way; but the measure bends between speed and share, and the item asks about one occasion while the options grade a whole shift.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the phones. How did calling back the guests whose calls rang out go? All called back within the hour · All called back that same day · Only some called back · Hardly any called back · None called back, those bookings lost · or: Someone else did the callbacks.
